name: TOML
vendor: toml-lang project, started by Tom Preston-Werner (open specification)
summary: A minimal configuration format with explicit types that maps unambiguously to a hash table; the language of `Cargo.toml` and `pyproject.toml`.
intro: A TOML file is a list of `key = value` lines grouped under `[table]` headers, which become nested hash tables when parsed; `[[name]]` starts another entry in an array of tables, and dotted keys such as `server.port = 8080` are shorthand for nesting. Every value has an explicit type you can see: strings are always quoted, and the other types are integers, floats, booleans, arrays, inline tables and four date and time types, from offset date-times to local times. Because nothing is guessed, `country = NO` is a syntax error, not `false`. Files must be UTF-8, keys are case-sensitive, `#` starts a comment, and defining the same table twice is an error.

The spec is maintained in the toml-lang/toml repository on GitHub under the MIT licence, with implementations in most languages. Version 1.0.0 (January 2021) was the first stable release; 1.1.0 (December 2025) allows newlines and trailing commas in inline tables, makes seconds optional in times and leaves integer size up to implementations, recommending at least 64 bits. Rust’s Cargo reads `Cargo.toml`, Python packaging reads `pyproject.toml`, and Python has shipped a read-only parser, `tomllib`, since 3.11; the 3.15 release candidates move it to TOML 1.1.
strengths: No implicit typing: strings are quoted and dates are a real type, so values mean what they look like
Comments and a flat, INI-like look make it easy to edit by hand
Maps unambiguously to a hash table, and redefining a key or table is an error rather than a silent override
The standard for Rust (`Cargo.toml`) and Python packaging (`pyproject.toml`), with a parser in Python’s standard library
limits: Deeply nested data gets verbose: every level needs a dotted header or an inline table, so it suits configuration, not data exchange
No anchors, references or includes; repeated settings are written out again
No schema language in the spec, so validation depends on each tool
Python’s `tomllib` can only read; writing, or editing a file while keeping its comments, needs a third-party library
1.1.0 syntax such as multi-line inline tables fails in parsers that only implement 1.0.0, including Python up to 3.14

story: In February 2013 Tom Preston-Werner, then GitHub’s co-founder and CEO, made the first commit to a small spec he called Tom’s Obvious, Minimal Language. The README explained why: “we need a decent human readable format that maps to a hash and the YAML spec is like 80 pages long and gives me rage. No, JSON doesn’t count. You know why.” Version 0.1.0 was tagged that March.

Rust’s package manager, Cargo, adopted it for `Cargo.toml`. In 2016, PEP 518 chose TOML for Python’s new `pyproject.toml` because it was human-usable, flexible, came from a standard and wasn’t overly complex like YAML, noting that the Rust community was “quite happy” with the choice. After years of 0.x releases and three release candidates, TOML 1.0.0 shipped in January 2021, and Python 3.11 added `tomllib` the next year. TOML 1.1.0 followed in December 2025, relaxing inline tables and date-time syntax.

choices.choice: Map unambiguously to a hash table
choices.why: The stated objective from the first README. Every key path has one meaning, so defining a key or table twice is an error instead of a silent override.
The first example carried the comment “First class dates? Why not?”. Quoting every string means a parser never has to guess, which avoids YAML’s implicit-typing surprises.
TOML’s own site says “all config files should support comments”, and the example in the very first README opened with one.
